2.1.3 Extending Risk Assessments Through Vulnerability Scans

Risks should be validated through vulnerability scans. These, also sometimes called pentesting,

detect weaknesses in the system by scanning for missing updates, patches,6 or existing

misconfigurations. Vulnerability scans should be conducted at planned intervals (for example,

annually) and when significant changes to port systems occur. They should be accompanied by an

updated risk register, which is a prioritized inventory of the most significant risks to achieving the

set objectives. It is maintained to track ownership and due dates for risk mitigation actions and to

monitor any changes to risk levels. Examples of risk mitigation actions, as well as further technical

resources for the reader, are provided in Appendix 3: Further Resources to Improve Protection.

In high-income settings, almost 69 percent of respondents conduct vulnerability scans or more

2.3 Main Takeaways and Key Recommendations

Many ports struggle to maintain a current risk picture and implement security controls into

routine operations across IT/OT. At the same time, incident readiness remains under-practiced and

insufficiently integrated with business continuity. A central challenge of cybersecurity in ports is

the transition from one-off risk-gauging efforts to continuous outcomes-focused risk management

(IMO 2025). By integrating cybersecurity responsibilities into established processes, such as risk

management, operations oversight, business continuity planning, and procurement, ports can

strengthen resilience without creating parallel institutional frameworks.

Box 3 Cybersecurity considerations within the ISPS Code

The ISPS Code is structured in two parts:

• Part A sets out mandatory requirements, including the obligation for port facilities to

conduct a Port Facility Security Assessment and to develop, implement, and maintain

an approved Port Facility Security Plan. The latter defines measures to prevent, detect,

and respond to security threats affecting port infrastructure, operations, personnel,

and cargo.

• Part B provides non-mandatory guidance on how to meet the requirements of Part A,

including illustrative examples of risks and mitigation measures.

Despite its broad governance scope, the ISPS Code was designed primarily to address

physical security risks and has undergone only limited updates since its adoption.

Cybersecurity is not included among the mandatory requirements in Part A. References

2.2.2 Practicing Business Continuity Plans

To be effective, incident response and business continuity plans should be regularly practiced and

tested through tabletop exercises and drills with clearly defined recovery time and recovery point

objectives. The literature on port resilience recommends practicing switching back to manual

operations7 to ensure a port’s ability to maintain degraded operations without core IT/OT systems

for extended periods (Varley et al. 2024).
